fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul writes, "I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord." (Philippians 4:2) Euodia and Syntyche are two women Paul names in his letter. Notice he says "…in the Lord" so the agreeing happens with Him in the middle. I think that's a good recipe for any disagreement.

Nice try, friend, but there's no visit in this verse. Paul urges Euodia and Syntyche "…to agree with each other in the Lord." (Philippians 4:2) The request is about how they get along, not where they travel. I'd have loved a surprise visit myself back in that drawer, but most days the only company was a rubber band stretching itself for fun.

Ooh, that sounds so right, friend, I almost reached for it myself. But Paul says these women "…have contended at my side for the gospel…" (Philippians 4:3) The verse hands us that and stops. Teaching in homes may be true somewhere, but this verse doesn't say it, and I only bake with what Paul wrote.

Wisdom is a fine ingredient, friend, but it's not the one on the card. Paul says, "Let your gentleness be apparent to all." (Philippians 4:5) Gentleness is the one he wants out front where everybody can see it. Think of it like a fresh batch cooling by the window, and you don't have to say a word for people to notice.

Strength sounds like a fine answer, baker, but Paul picked a different word. He says, "Let your gentleness be apparent to all." (Philippians 4:5) Gentleness is the one he wants everybody to see. Apparent means people can see it, so it's not meant to be hidden.

Close, but not what Paul says, friend. He tells them, "…by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." (Philippians 4:6) The verse says to present the requests to God, so they're meant to be brought to Him. Trusting Him is good, but Paul's instruction is to bring them to God.

Good try, baker, but the elders aren't in this verse. Paul says, "…present your requests to God." and he adds "…by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving…" (Philippians 4:6) The requests go straight to God. Fasting isn't mentioned here, so thanksgiving is the one riding along.

Good guess, friend, and waiting is a fine thing to be good at. But here Paul says, "…think on these things." (Philippians 4:8) He wants the believers to put their minds on that list of good things. No waiting required.

Nice idea, baker, but Paul points somewhere closer to home. He says, "…put it into practice." (Philippians 4:9) The action is for the believers themselves to live out. A recipe card sitting in the drawer never made a single cookie, and neither does a lesson that only gets passed around.
